KEY MESSAGE 1...

In the mid/upper-levels, the center of the subtropical ridge, which 
was objectively analyzed at 600 dam per the 12Z UA charts, was 
located over the Lower MS River Valley and continues to retrograde 
westward. Farther north, a well-defined shortwave trough was digging 
southeastward towards the James Bay, with the base of the intense 
jetlets translating over the Great Lakes region. Several series of 
smaller-scale perturbations were progressing eastward over the Rust 
Belt and have generated a few bands of general thunderstorms across 
the northern counties over the last few hours. GOES-East visible 
trends have recently shown additional bands of congested cu forming 
to the north of the I-64 corridor between CRW-HTS due the subtle 
influence of an ejecting shortwave perturbation overhead. There also 
appears to be a trapped mountain wave on water-vapor imagery that is 
aiding in the formation of the diurnally-driven cu. The 12Z RAOB 
from WFO ILN sampled a stout EML, characterized by SB/MUCAPE values 
exceeding 3,000 J/kg and an equilibrium level up to 125 mb within 
the belt of broadly cyclonic flow. However, farther southeast at 
RNK, large-scale subsidence remained intact atop the lower tranche 
of the EML advecting over the Appalachian Mountains, which should 
keep the cu field suppressed until peak heating is reached. The 
subtropical ridge will continue retrograding over the next 24 hours, 
which will keep the CWA positioned along the edge of the thickness 
gradient and south of the more-intense flow aloft through Friday.

At the surface, the quasi-stationary front remained along and north 
of the I-70 corridor, but has since become convectively-reinforced, 
and will begin sagging southward into southeastern OH and northern 
WV by this evening. Ahead of the front, the airmass is essentially a 
clone of yesterday less some convective cloud debris, with dewpoints 
in the lower-middle 70s and hot surface temperatures that have 
breached 90 degrees, particularly in the OH River Valley. This will 
result in heat indices in the middle 90s to near 100 degrees for 
some locales this afternoon, and the SPS highlighting the heat and 
high humidity has been reissued through 23Z, or 7 PM EDT, this 
evening for portions of the lowlands. Additional storm development 
is expected across the lowlands through this evening due to the 
uncapped airmass, with the mean convective movement governed by 
propagation along any boundaries. Heavy rainfall will be the primary 
hazard, leading to localized instances of flash flooding. Following 
sunset, there will be a temporary lull in showers and storms until 
the cold front arrives during the overnight hours.

As the cold front arrives, another shortwave impulse will propagate 
over the CWA, with indications pointing towards the potential for 
semi-organized bands of training storms to develop along the slow, 
southward-moving cold front. Corfidi vectors favor frontal-parallel 
back-building of individual cells while the total propagation vector 
orients southward along the edge of the thickness gradient. The 
tall, skinny CAPE profiles; anomalously high PWAT content, meager 
length of the shear vectors, and moist-adiabatic lapse rates will 
galvanize the heavy rain potential with storms tonight into the 
predawn hours Friday. However, there exists uncertainty with respect 
to the spatiotemporal extent of storms during the early morning 
hours Friday. As a result, confidence is still not high enough to 
warrant the issuance of a Flood Watch, although it will continue to 
be evaluated in forthcoming prognostications. The severe weather 
threat is otherwise low, but a strong wind gust or two cannot be 
ruled out with collapsing cores overnight.

KEY MESSAGE 2...

Storm chances will wane from north-to-south after sunrise Friday, 
with an expectation for river valley fog to return following storms 
late tonight and an overcast sky lasting into the afternoon hours 
across most of the CWA. Northwesterly flow will advect over the CWA 
by mid-day Friday as the shortwave trough currently digging into the 
James Bay ejects eastward towards the Canadian Maritimes. Elevated, 
post-frontal showers may develop across portions of the lowlands and 
mountains during the afternoon hours Friday, with better chances for 
lightning across the Coal Fields, which will be in closer proximity 
to the departing cold front. The flash flooding potential is very 
low Friday nor is severe weather expected with any renegade cells 
that develop Friday afternoon. Highs are expected to be a few 
degrees cooler area-wide Friday, albeit still very warm, with heat 
indices peaking in the lower 90s for the southwestern zones. 

The cold front is forecast to clear to the south of the CWA late 
Friday night and become quasi-stationary once again as the 
subtropical ridge flattens via a neutrally-tilted shortwave trough
